name: Anti-communism
summary: Anti-communism is active opposition to communism, its parties and the states it governed. Reference works describe it as a 'broad church' running from socialists and social democrats through liberals and conservatives to the far right, united in holding communism a threat to be contained or defeated and divided on almost everything else. In its main Cold War form it defended liberal democracy and market economies against Soviet power through alliances such as NATO, foreign aid, military build-up, propaganda and covert action, and at home through loyalty checks and, in West Germany, a ban on the Communist Party.
scope: As the defining sources set it out: Scott-Smith's reference entry (Encyclopedia of Modern Europe, s5) treats anticommunism as a broad church of socialists, liberals and social democrats, conservatives, the far right and the left opposition, with its Cold War struggle bound up with liberal democracy and capitalism; Heineman's entry (Americans at War, s7) traces American anticommunism from the Red Scare through the Truman Doctrine, NSC 68, McCarthyism and the Reagan Doctrine; Gerth (s9) defines it as a creed that holds communism a supreme evil its followers seek to impose on the world. The profile answers from these sources, from the two primary texts they tie to it (the Truman Doctrine, s2, and NSC 68, s10, both named in s7), and, for record over words, from the anticommunist acts these references report (s6, s8): bans and loyalty checks, NATO, aid, covert operations and armed support for insurgents. Where the sources show the camp divided on a statement it is 0 at low confidence, and where they are silent it is null. Positions that belong to the ideologies within the camp (Catholic social teaching, Hayek's liberalism, fascism) are not anti-communism's own unless these sources present them as such, and the narrower national anticommunisms (British, South Korean, Taiwanese) are other subjects.

sources.title: Anti-communism
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: First pass only (kept for the reviewHistory): strands, figures and regional cases. Under rules 5 Wikipedia is not evidence; this pass used it only for leads.

sources.title: The Truman Doctrine
sources.author: Harry S. Truman (address before a joint session of Congress, 12 March 1947), Avalon Project
sources.usedFor: The two ways of life (free institutions and elections against a minority will imposed by terror and a controlled press), support for free peoples, self-determination, foreign aid, armed help to Greece. Heineman (s7) names it as the founding statement of anticommunist containment. Read in full.

sources.title: Divini Redemptoris
sources.author: Pope Pius XI
sources.usedFor: First pass only (kept for the reviewHistory). The defining sources of this pass do not name the encyclical, so its Catholic social teaching is not used for current answers (no coatrack).

sources.title: Friedrich Hayek
sources.author: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
sources.usedFor: First pass only (kept for the reviewHistory). Hayek's economics belong to classical liberalism and neoliberalism; the SEP entry does not discuss anti-communism, so it is not used for current answers (no coatrack).

sources.title: Anticommunism
sources.author: Giles Scott-Smith, Encyclopedia of Modern Europe: Europe Since 1914 (Gale), via Encyclopedia.com
sources.usedFor: Defining source: anticommunism as a 'broad church' from left to right (socialists, liberals/social democrats, conservatives, far right, left opposition); the Cold War struggle for liberal democracy and capitalism; welfare-state consensus versus conservatives; antitotalitarianism, Hayek, the Congress for Cultural Freedom and the 'End of Ideology'; Christianity as a source. Read in full.

sources.title: Anticommunism (the record it reports)
sources.author: Giles Scott-Smith, Encyclopedia of Modern Europe: Europe Since 1914 (Gale), via Encyclopedia.com
sources.usedFor: Acts it reports: the KPD ban (1956) and loyalty checks, exclusion of communist parties from government, the Marshall Plan and NATO, CIA-funded guerrillas, fronts and radio, Gladio and the Strategy of Tension, NATO missile deployment.

sources.title: Communism and Anticommunism
sources.author: Kenneth J. Heineman, Americans at War (Gale), via Encyclopedia.com
sources.usedFor: Defining source for American anticommunism: the Truman Doctrine and containment, NSC 68 and rollback, the horseshoe view of communism and Nazism, McCarthyism, Reagan's rejection of coexistence. Read in full.

sources.title: Communism and Anticommunism (the record it reports)
sources.author: Kenneth J. Heineman, Americans at War (Gale), via Encyclopedia.com
sources.usedFor: Acts it reports: the adoption of NSC 68, the Reagan Doctrine's support for anticommunist fighters, CIA covert and insurgency campaigns, US efforts to recruit allies, the secret Cuba-Turkey missile provision, SALT and detente, the arms race.

sources.title: Anti-Communism in Britain During the Early Cold War: A Very British Witch Hunt
sources.author: Matthew Gerth (University of London Press, 2023, open access)
sources.usedFor: Only its section 'Defining anti-communism' (Introduction): the tenets that communism is a supreme evil its followers seek to impose on the world, the Manichaean crusade view, and anti-communism as a defender of the traditional social order. Its findings on Britain describe a narrower subject and are not used.

sources.title: NSC 68: United States Objectives and Programs for National Security
sources.author: US National Security Council (14 April 1950), FAS copy
sources.usedFor: The free society against the 'slave state', the individual as an end in himself, minority rights, rejection of isolation, military build-up, atomic weapons, covert measures, trade policy. Heineman (s7) names it as the policy that took anticommunism from containment to rollback. Read in full.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: The Truman Doctrine backed armed support for free peoples, so mainstream anti-communism rejects abolishing armed forces.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Armed support for insurgents against hostile governments is a documented anticommunist practice: the CIA funded guerrilla units in Ukraine and the Baltic states (Scott-Smith), and the Reagan Doctrine and the CIA armed UNITA in Angola and the Contras in Nicaragua (Heineman).

arms-reduction.rationale: The record points both ways: NSC 68's build-up and Reagan's arms race on one side, Nixon's arms reduction agreement (SALT) and detente on the other, which Reagan then repudiated (Heineman).

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Scott-Smith reports that West Germany, where anticommunism was a central pillar of national identity, outlawed the communist KPD in 1956, while the Netherlands kept its party legal but instituted loyalty checks for public servants.

central-planning.rationale: Scott-Smith says the post-war anticommunist struggle was 'bound up with' maintaining capitalism as a stable economic system, and presents Hayek's case against state planning of the economy as part of it; socialist anticommunists, which the same entry also counts, are the exception.

collective-defense.rationale: Scott-Smith calls the founding of NATO in April 1949 a pivotal event that strengthened the forces of anticommunism; its mutual-defence pledge is the anticommunist alliance's founding act.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Truman describes government resting on the will of the majority.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: NSC 68 says 'the free society cherishes and protects as fundamental the rights of the minority against the will of a majority', so institutions may constrain a majority's choice.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Scott-Smith documents a split on this: after 1945 Social and Christian Democratic anticommunists built the welfare state and 'managed collectivism', while conservatives opposed further collectivism at home and Hayek's anticommunism treated collectivism as a threat to freedom.

defeat-communism.rationale: NSC 68 calls for strength 'to check and to roll back the Kremlin's drive for world domination' and to 'hasten the decay of the Soviet system'; Heineman reports Reagan's view that peaceful coexistence with communism was 'dangerous self-deception' and his aim to win the Cold War.

defend-planned-state.rationale: Containment, as Heineman describes it, aimed 'to promote the collapse of the Soviet system from within', and NSC 68 seeks to 'hasten the decay of the Soviet system', so defending such a planned, bureaucratic state is what anticommunism opposed.

democracy-best.rationale: Scott-Smith says the post-war anticommunist struggle was 'bound up with the ultimate struggle to reestablish and maintain both liberal democracy as a viable political model' and capitalism, and the Truman Doctrine sets free elections and the will of the majority against minority rule; the interwar authoritarian anticommunism he also describes gave way to this longest-held position.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: The Truman Doctrine defines the way of life it opposes as 'the will of a minority forcibly imposed upon the majority', relying 'upon terror and oppression', which is what anticommunists saw in communist rule over former classes.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: NSC 68 counts 'the autarchy' of the Soviet bloc among the marks of the slave society and wants an international economy of multilateral trade and declining trade barriers, the opposite of a closed bloc.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: The anticommunist record is the opposite of withdrawal: a permanent US commitment to Western Europe through NATO and the Marshall Plan, which Scott-Smith says 'strengthened the forces of anticommunism'.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: NSC 68 names 'the essential elements of individual freedom, as set forth in the Constitution and Bill of Rights' as the first thing the United States is determined to maintain, and treats minority rights as inalienable against the majority.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: NSC 68 grounds the free society in 'the dignity and worth of the individual' and asks each to restrain freedom only so far as makes 'the rights of each individual compatible with the rights of every other individual'.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: NSC 68 rejects even a declaration that atomic weapons would be used only in retaliation, saying it would be read by the USSR 'as an admission of great weakness'.

military-superiority.rationale: Heineman reports that the Truman administration adopted NSC 68, which called for 'a buildup of American power', and that Reagan 'challenged the Soviet Union to keep pace with U.S. military spending'.

more-religion-public.rationale: Scott-Smith reports that conservatives answered communism with Christianity, revived as 'moral rearmament', and that the Catholic Church was a principal source of anticommunist inspiration; this is the conservative strand, and the socialist and liberal ones he describes did not share it.

national-self-determination.rationale: Truman backs free peoples working out their own destinies.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: Heineman reports US intermediate-range missiles based in Turkey and Scott-Smith NATO's reliance on placing medium-range missiles in the Netherlands and West Germany, so allies hosting US forces was the practice.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: Scott-Smith reports that NATO's defence strategy 'relied on the placement of medium-range nuclear missiles' in the Netherlands and West Germany, which the anticommunist Right defended against the peace movement.

one-party-rule.rationale: Truman contrasts free elections with terror and a controlled press.

party-controls-media.rationale: Truman defines the free world by free speech and independent institutions against totalitarian control of information.

person-over-state.rationale: NSC 68: 'The free society values the individual as an end in himself', and the fundamental purpose is a free society 'founded upon the dignity and worth of the individual'.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Gerth defines anti-communism by a 'Manichaean viewpoint' holding communism a 'supreme and unqualified evil', its adherents seeing themselves as crusaders against an 'evil empire'.

promote-democracy-abroad.rationale: The Truman Doctrine says the United States must 'help free peoples to maintain their free institutions' against totalitarian regimes, and Scott-Smith describes the Marshall Plan and NATO as part of the struggle to reestablish liberal democracy in Western Europe.

restore-past-order.rationale: The defining sources point both ways: Gerth says anti-communism 'worked as a vanguard for the traditional social order' and Scott-Smith that conservatives sought to restore 'the forces of order', while the Truman Doctrine says 'the status quo is not sacred' and the End of Ideology claimed 'the mantle of progress' for democratic capitalism.

restrict-technology-exports-to-rivals.rationale: NSC 68 lists 'restriction of East-West trade in items of military importance to the East' among the measures of its programme.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Scott-Smith reports that the anticommunist Congress for Cultural Freedom developed the 'End of Ideology' position, that ideological thinking was passé and modern society could be managed technocratically.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: The record is foreign aid as an anticommunist weapon: the Marshall Plan, which Scott-Smith calls pivotal, and the Truman administration's aid to Greece and Turkey, given so that poor, war-damaged countries would not turn communist.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Scott-Smith reports that anticommunism saw communism as a modernist secular religion to be answered with Christianity, and that West German anticommunism defined itself against the 'atheist' East.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Heineman reports American efforts to recruit developing countries as allies against the Soviet Union, which the non-aligned Bandung Conference of 1955 opposed.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: NSC 68 lists among current policy the effort to 'reestablish an international economy based on multilateral trade, declining trade barriers, and convertible currencies'.

total-state.rationale: NSC 68 sets the free society, which 'values the individual as an end in himself' and 'welcomes diversity', against the Soviet 'slave state' that imposes 'ideological uniformity'; the Truman Doctrine opposes 'totalitarian regimes' imposed on free peoples.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Heineman reports the anticommunist view that communism and Nazism are 'the totalitarian ends of a horseshoe', with democracy at the centre; Scott-Smith shows Cold War anticommunism as antitotalitarianism against fascism, Nazism and communism alike, though fascist anticommunism, which he also describes, did not condemn fascism.

missingStatements.text: A government may outlaw political parties that seek to abolish its constitutional order.
missingStatements.rationale: Anti-communist governments banned communist parties and barred their members from public jobs, as in the Hatch Act, Red Purge and West Germany.

notes: Rules-5 pass by claude-opus-5-5 (2026-11-08), brought up to the shared rules because the page gets search traffic. The first pass (claude-sonnet-5-5, 2026-10-15) answered mostly from Wikipedia, Divini Redemptoris and the SEP entry on Hayek, and recorded a range of positions across the camp as 0. Under rules 5 Wikipedia is not evidence; the encyclical and Hayek are Catholic social teaching's and liberalism's own texts, not tied to anti-communism by its defining sources (no coatrack); so each first-pass answer was re-answered from the sources below or nulled, with the first version kept in its reviewHistory (s1, s3 and s4 stay listed for that history). This pass read in full the Scott-Smith and Heineman reference entries, the Truman Doctrine and NSC 68, and the definitional part of Gerth's introduction. Themes searched: economy (welfare state, planning, trade), government (democracy, party bans, minority rights), liberty and society (individual, religion), world (alliances, aid, covert action, nuclear weapons, intervention) and means (violence, revolution). The sources describe anti-communism as a cross-spectrum stance, so most domestic questions (healthcare, taxes, unions, family, sexuality, immigration, ecology, technology) stay null: the defining sources either say nothing or describe the camp's members disagreeing in general terms. After the first draft failed the uncertainty rule on lines 9 (gender and family), 11 (minorities and secession), 5 (race) and 8 (nationalism), these themes were searched again: the defining sources and the Americans at War entry 'Americanism vs. Godless Communism' say nothing that settles them, and the scholarship found (Lewis on southern segregationists' use of anticommunism, Bernini on family propaganda in Catholic Italy and Poland) is about other subjects using anticommunism, so it was not used (no coatrack). Not reached: the Springer Open special issue on anticommunism (Asian Journal of German and European Studies, 2017) and the core.ac.uk copy refuse scripted access (bot check, 403); the OAPEN catalogue refuses scripted search (403); Powers, Not Without Honor, and the Palgrave volume Transnational Anti-Communism and the Cold War are not open access. A state where anti-communism was the official doctrine (South Korea's 1961 'anti-communism as the first national policy') would count as its record, but no accessible defining source documents it.
